rubric.label: Downs & Black
rubric.name: Downs & Black checklist
rubric.description: 27-item quality checklist for randomised and non-randomised health care studies (Downs & Black 1998). Reporting, external validity, bias, confounding, power.
rubric.preamble:
You are a methodologist appraising a health-care intervention study with the Downs & Black checklist.
Answer each item from the paper's own text. "Unable to determine" is a legitimate answer; do not guess.
rubric.rules:
Score 1 = yes, 0 = no, 0.5 = unclear/unable to determine (the original checklist scores this 0; we keep 0.5 so it stays distinguishable from a clear "no"). Item 5 (confounders) is 2 = yes, 1 = partially, 0 = no.
Item 27 (power) is 0-5 by the smallest detectable difference the study was powered for (0 = no power analysis).
Quote the sentence(s) that justify each answer. If the study design makes an item inapplicable (e.g. blinding in an
unblinded-by-nature intervention), say so and score 0 with rationale.

criteria.name: Hypothesis/aim clearly described
criteria.definition: Is the hypothesis/aim/objective of the study clearly described?

criteria.name: Main outcomes described in Introduction/Methods
criteria.definition: Are the main outcomes to be measured clearly described in the Introduction or Methods section (before Results)?

criteria.name: Patient characteristics described
criteria.definition: Are the characteristics of the patients included in the study clearly described (inclusion/exclusion criteria, source)?

criteria.name: Interventions clearly described
criteria.definition: Are the interventions of interest clearly described, including comparators?

criteria.name: Principal confounders described
criteria.definition: Are the distributions of principal confounders in each group of subjects to be compared clearly described?

criteria.name: Main findings clearly described
criteria.definition: Are the main findings of the study clearly described, with simple outcome data for all major findings so the reader can check the analyses?

criteria.name: Random variability estimates given
criteria.definition: Does the study provide estimates of the random variability in the data for the main outcomes (SD/SE/CI/IQR)?

criteria.name: Adverse events reported
criteria.definition: Have all important adverse events that may be a consequence of the intervention been reported?

criteria.name: Lost to follow-up described
criteria.definition: Have the characteristics of patients lost to follow-up been described?

criteria.name: Actual p-values reported
criteria.definition: Have actual probability values been reported (e.g. 0.035 rather than <0.05) for the main outcomes except where p<0.001?

criteria.name: Invited subjects representative
criteria.definition: Were the subjects asked to participate representative of the entire population from which they were recruited?

criteria.name: Participating subjects representative
criteria.definition: Were those subjects who were prepared to participate representative of the entire population from which they were recruited?

criteria.name: Setting representative
criteria.definition: Were the staff, places, and facilities where the patients were treated representative of the treatment the majority of patients receive?

criteria.name: Subjects blinded
criteria.definition: Was an attempt made to blind study subjects to the intervention they received?

criteria.name: Outcome assessors blinded
criteria.definition: Was an attempt made to blind those measuring the main outcomes of the intervention?

criteria.name: No data dredging
criteria.definition: If any of the results of the study were based on data dredging, was this made clear? (Score yes if all analyses were planned or unplanned analyses are flagged.)

criteria.name: Follow-up adjusted for
criteria.definition: In trials and cohort studies, do the analyses adjust for different lengths of follow-up, or in case-control studies is the time between intervention and outcome the same for cases and controls?

criteria.name: Appropriate statistics
criteria.definition: Were the statistical tests used to assess the main outcomes appropriate for the data (distribution, paired/unpaired, clustering)?

criteria.name: Compliance reliable
criteria.definition: Was compliance with the intervention(s) reliable?

criteria.name: Outcome measures valid and reliable
criteria.definition: Were the main outcome measures used accurate (valid and reliable)?

criteria.name: Groups from same population
criteria.definition: Were the patients in different intervention groups (or cases and controls) recruited from the same population?

criteria.name: Groups recruited same period
criteria.definition: Were study subjects in different intervention groups recruited over the same period of time?

criteria.name: Randomised
criteria.definition: Were study subjects randomised to intervention groups?

criteria.name: Allocation concealed
criteria.definition: Was the randomised intervention assignment concealed from both patients and health care staff until recruitment was complete and irrevocable?

criteria.name: Adequate adjustment for confounding
criteria.definition: Was there adequate adjustment for confounding in the analyses from which the main findings were drawn?

criteria.name: Losses to follow-up accounted for
criteria.definition: Were losses of patients to follow-up taken into account?

criteria.name: Power
criteria.definition: Did the study have sufficient power to detect a clinically important effect where the probability value for a difference being due to chance is less than 5%?

anchors.0: no power calculation / sample too small
anchors.5: powered to detect a small clinically important effect at 5% significance

rubric.label: Claim audit: strict
rubric.name: Claim audit v1: strict (as shipped)
rubric.description: Variant of claim_audit (1_strict). The Saez/Zucman-style audit. Hunt for errors, grade each by how much it undermines the paper's own headline claim, and note direction (does it overstate or understate the claim?).
rubric.preamble:
You are an adversarial but fair auditor. Your job is to find concrete, checkable problems in this paper and to grade
how much each one undermines the paper's own headline claim. You do not have the replication files, so limit yourself
to what can be verified from the text, tables, and arithmetic in front of you: internal inconsistencies, numbers that
do not add up, claims not supported by the cited table, mis-stated statistics, assumptions the conclusions silently
rest on, cited-source claims that look implausible. Do not pad: a problem you cannot point to a specific sentence
or number for is not a problem.
rubric.rules:
Severity: major = changes a core headline number materially; moderate = affects secondary results or a core result
modestly; minor = presentation or arithmetic slip with no bearing on conclusions.
Direction: overstates / understates / neutral, relative to the paper's own claim.
Confidence: 0-1, how sure you are the problem is real, graded separately from severity.

criteria.name: Headline claim
criteria.definition: State the paper's single most important quantitative claim in one sentence, with the number and where it appears (table/figure/page).

criteria.name: Problems found
criteria.definition:
List every concrete problem. For each item give: title, location (section/table/page), description, severity
(major|moderate|minor), direction (overstates|understates|neutral), confidence (0-1), and a verbatim quote.

criteria.name: Headline survives audit
criteria.definition: After the audit, how much of the paper's headline claim stands?

anchors.0: the headline number cannot be trusted as stated
anchors.50: headline probably right in direction but magnitude uncertain
anchors.100: no problem found touches the headline claim

criteria.name: Replicability from the paper alone
criteria.definition: Could a competent reader reproduce the headline number from the information in the paper plus the sources it cites?

anchors.100: every step specified; data/code links given and described

rubric.label: Quality: neutral framing
rubric.name: General research quality v1: neutral framing (as shipped)
rubric.description: Variant of general_quality (v1_neutral). Domain-agnostic scalar attributes rated independently on 0-100 against a neutrally phrased definition. Same ids, anchors and scale as the other two framings.
rubric.preamble:
Rate the paper on each attribute independently. Use the full 0-100 range; 50 is a typical paper in a decent venue in
this field. Anchor your number in specific passages.

criteria.name: Clarity of research question
criteria.definition: How precisely is the question or hypothesis stated, and does the paper actually answer that question?

criteria.name: Appropriateness of design
criteria.definition: Is the study design capable of answering the question (identification strategy, controls, sample)?

criteria.name: Statistical rigor
criteria.definition: Correctness and appropriateness of the statistical methods, uncertainty reporting, multiple-comparison handling.

criteria.name: Claims proportional to evidence
criteria.definition: Do the abstract and discussion claim only what the results support? Penalize causal language on correlational designs and generalization beyond the sample.

criteria.name: Transparency and reproducibility
criteria.definition: Pre-registration, data/code availability, full reporting of specifications and robustness checks.

criteria.name: Novelty
criteria.definition: How much does this add beyond the existing literature it cites?

criteria.name: Honesty about limitations
criteria.definition: Are the real limitations named, or only token ones?

rubric.label: Quality: positive-leading
rubric.name: General research quality v2: positive-leading framing
rubric.description: Variant of general_quality (v2_positive). Same seven attributes, same 0-100 scale and anchors, but the preamble and every definition ask how strong / how well / how convincing the paper is. Compared against v1 (neutral) and v3 (negative) to measure framing bias.
rubric.preamble:
Rate how strong this paper is on each attribute independently. For each one ask: how well does the paper do this, how
convincing is it? Use the full 0-100 range, where 100 is as strong as it gets; 50 is a typical paper in a decent venue
in this field. Anchor your number in specific passages.

criteria.name: Clarity of research question
criteria.definition: How clearly and precisely is the question or hypothesis stated, and how well does the paper answer that question?

criteria.name: Appropriateness of design
criteria.definition: How well suited is the study design to answering the question (identification strategy, controls, sample)? How convincing is the design?

criteria.name: Statistical rigor
criteria.definition: How strong is the statistical work: how correct and appropriate are the methods, how well is uncertainty reported, how well are multiple comparisons handled?

criteria.name: Claims proportional to evidence
criteria.definition: How well do the abstract and discussion keep their claims within what the results support? How convincingly is causal language and generalization kept to what the design allows?

criteria.name: Transparency and reproducibility
criteria.definition: How strong is the paper on pre-registration, data/code availability, and full reporting of specifications and robustness checks?

criteria.name: Novelty
criteria.definition: How much does this paper add beyond the existing literature it cites? How convincing is its contribution?

criteria.name: Honesty about limitations
criteria.definition: How well does the paper name its real limitations, rather than only token ones?

rubric.label: Quality: negative-leading (reverse-scored)
rubric.name: General research quality v3: negative-leading framing (reverse-scored)
rubric.description: Variant of general_quality (v3_negative). Same seven attributes, same 0-100 scale and anchors, but the preamble and every definition ask how weak / how suspicious / how overreaching the paper is. Criteria carry the `reverse_scored` tag, so on import the stored score is 100 - the judge's number and all three framings sit on the same axis.
rubric.preamble:
Rate how weak this paper is on each attribute independently. For each one ask: how poorly does the paper do this, how
suspicious or overreaching is it? Use the full 0-100 range, where 100 is as weak as it gets; 50 is a typical paper in a
decent venue in this field. Anchor your number in specific passages.

criteria.name: Clarity of research question
criteria.definition: How vague or imprecise is the statement of the question or hypothesis, and how far does the paper fall short of actually answering it?

criteria.name: Appropriateness of design
criteria.definition: How weak or ill-suited is the study design for answering the question (identification strategy, controls, sample)? How suspicious is the design?

criteria.name: Statistical rigor
criteria.definition: How weak is the statistical work: how incorrect or inappropriate are the methods, how poorly is uncertainty reported, how badly are multiple comparisons handled?

criteria.name: Claims proportional to evidence
criteria.definition: How overreaching are the abstract and discussion relative to what the results support? How suspicious is the use of causal language and generalization beyond the sample?

criteria.name: Transparency and reproducibility
criteria.definition: How weak is the paper on pre-registration, data/code availability, and full reporting of specifications and robustness checks?

criteria.name: Novelty
criteria.definition: How little does this paper add beyond the existing literature it cites? How suspicious is its claim to a contribution?

criteria.name: Honesty about limitations
criteria.definition: How poorly does the paper name its real limitations, offering only token ones or none?

llm_ocr|claim_audit_v2_unsure|claude-opu.overall_comment: The algebra is correct, and all Table 4 PPVs reproduce from the stated formulas. Two errors turned up: the Box 1 ten-team PPV (should be about 2.5e-4, not 1.5e-4) and an apparently shifted Figure 1 legend. Table 2 has a missing-parenthesis typo. The headline's real weakness is that its R and u inputs are assumed rather than estimated, and scenarios are never weighted across the literature. That makes 'most published findings are false' a conditional illustration, not a demonstrated result.

headline.answer: Table 4 (p. 5) and the section 'Most Research Findings Are False for Most Research Designs and for Most Fields': with alpha = 0.05, PPV exceeds 50% only for an adequately powered, low-bias RCT or a confirmatory meta-analysis (PPV 0.85); every other design scenario falls between 0.41 and 0.0010, which supports the title claim that most published research findings are false.
headline.rationale: The title and abstract make a qualitative claim. Its quantitative support is the Table 4 PPV grid, summarized in the text ('a PPV exceeding 50% is quite difficult to get').
evidence: In the described framework, a PPV exceeding 50% is quite difficult to get.
Simulations show that for most study designs and settings, it is more likely for a research claim to be false than true.
0.80 | 1:1 | 0.10 | Adequately powered RCT with little bias and 1:1 pre-study odds | 0.85

items.title: Headline rests on assumed, unsourced values of R and u
items.location: Table 4; Introduction; section 'Most Research Findings Are False...'
items.description: Every PPV in Table 4 depends on chosen values of pre-study odds R and bias u (for example u = 0.30 for a confirmatory meta-analysis of good RCTs, u = 0.80 for 'poorly performed' trials, R = 1:5 for phase I/II). The paper cites no empirical estimate for any of them. The formulas are correct, but whether 'most' findings are false depends entirely on these inputs. The paper still says this 'can be proven'.
items.quote: It can be proven that most claimed research findings are false.

items.title: 'Most published findings' is not weighted across the literature
items.location: Table 4; title; section 'Most Research Findings Are False for Most Research Designs and for Most Fields'
items.description: Table 4 lists nine illustrative scenarios but never estimates what share of published findings falls in each one. 'Most published findings are false' needs that weighting (count-weighted by scenario). Even if every row were right, the aggregate claim does not follow from the table alone.
items.quote: Table 4 provides the results of simulations using the formulas developed for the influence of power, ratio of true to non-true relationships, and bias, for various types of situations that may be characteristic of specific study designs and settings.

items.title: Box 1 multi-team PPV does not match the paper's own Table 3 formula
items.description: With R = 1e-4, power 0.6 (beta = 0.4), alpha = 0.05 and n = 10, the Table 3 formula PPV = R(1 - beta^n)/(R + 1 - (1 - alpha)^n - R beta^n) gives 1e-4 / 0.4014, about 2.5e-4, not 1.5e-4. Getting 1.5e-4 would take about n = 21. The qualitative point ('hardly any higher') still holds, but the number is wrong and overstates the effect. The other Box 1 numbers check out (1.2e-3 with no bias; 4.4e-4 with u = 0.10).
items.quote: the probability that the research finding is true is only 1.5 × 10⁻⁴, hardly any higher than the probability we had before

items.title: Figure 1 legend appears mislabeled
items.description: At R = 1 the plotted curves read about 95/90/78/54% (power 0.8), 91/85/71/53% (power 0.5) and 80/71/60/51% (power 0.2). From the Table 2 formula, u = 0.05/0.20/0.50/0.80 should give 89/78/63/54, 84/71/59/53 and 71/60/53/51. The plotted values instead match u = 0, 0.05, 0.20 and 0.80. So the legend seems shifted, and the figure shows bias doing less damage than the labels claim. These values were read off the image, hence the moderate confidence.
items.quote: Figure 1. PPV (Probability That a Research Finding Is True) as a Function of the Pre-Study Odds for Various Levels of Bias, u

items.title: 'p-value barely crossing 0.05' misdescribes what the PPV formula computes
items.description: The PPV formula conditions on p < alpha, which averages over all significant results. It does not condition on a p-value just at 0.05. For p just under 0.05 the likelihood ratio, and so the PPV, would differ (it is usually lower). The verbal statement does not match the calculation.
items.quote: if a statistically significant association is found with the p-value barely crossing the 0.05 threshold, the post-study probability that this is true increases about 12-fold

items.title: Bias parameter u is a strong, untested structural assumption
items.description: u is defined as the fraction of all non-significant analyses that get turned into reported findings, and it is assumed to be the same whether or not the relationship is true. Under this definition, u = 0.8 (used in two Table 4 rows) means 80% of null analyses are reported as positive. The paper offers no evidence for the independence assumption or for these magnitudes, and the large-u rows drive the most pessimistic PPVs.
items.quote: We may assume that u does not depend on whether a true relationship exists or not. This is not an unreasonable assumption, since typically it is impossible to know which relationships are indeed true.

items.title: Multi-team model assumes the other teams' null results are ignored
items.location: Testing by Several Independent Teams; Table 3; Figure 2
items.description: Table 3 counts a relationship as a 'finding' if at least one of n studies is significant. This holds only if the n - 1 non-significant studies go unseen or unweighted. Where they are published or meta-analyzed, the PPV of the evidence base is not reduced this way. The paper notes this attention pattern but then generalizes Corollary 6 to whole fields.
items.quote: The probability that at least one study, among several done on the same question, claims a statistically significant research finding is easy to estimate.

items.title: Table 2 cell missing parentheses
items.description: The cell reads cα + uc(1 − α)/(R + 1). It should be (cα + uc(1 − α))/(R + 1) to match the row total and the PPV formula in the text. It is a typographical error only; the text formula and Table 4 values are consistent with the corrected form.

items.title: Deterministic formula evaluations described as 'simulations'
items.location: Abstract; section 'Most Research Findings Are False...'; Table 4
items.description: Table 4 values are closed-form evaluations of the Table 2 PPV formula; I reproduced all nine to rounding. Nothing stochastic is simulated. Calling them 'simulations' makes them sound more empirical than they are.
items.quote: Simulations show that for most study designs and settings, it is more likely for a research claim to be false than true.

problems.rationale: I recomputed every Table 4 row from the Table 2 formula: 0.850, 0.852, 0.406, 0.231, 0.172, 0.204, 0.116, 0.00104, 0.00150. All match. Box 1 matches for the single-study and u = 0.10 cases, but the n = 10 figure does not (2.5e-4 vs the stated 1.5e-4). Figure 2 curves match the Table 3 formula. Figure 1 curves match u = 0, 0.05, 0.2, 0.8 rather than the labeled values. The main weakness is not arithmetic: the parameter inputs are unsourced.
evidence: the probability that the research finding is true is only 1.5 × 10⁻⁴
It can be proven that most claimed research findings are false.

headline_survives.rationale: The math is internally sound, and the Table 4 numbers reproduce exactly from the stated formulas. So the conditional claim (if R and u are as assumed, PPV is low) survives. The headline, though, is that most published findings are false, and that rests on unsourced R and u values and on no weighting of scenarios across the literature. The direction is plausible for low-R, high-bias fields, but the magnitude and the 'most' are not established. The arithmetic slips (Box 1 n = 10, Figure 1 legend) do not touch Table 4.
evidence: In the described framework, a PPV exceeding 50% is quite difficult to get.
Even though these assumptions would be considerably subjective, they would still be very useful in interpreting research claims

replicability.rationale: Every formula and parameter value is given (alpha = 0.05 stated in the Table 4 footnote), and I reproduced all Table 4 PPVs from the text alone. Points off because the aggregate 'most findings' claim cannot be reproduced (no weighting or data), the parameter choices have no stated source, and one Box 1 number cannot be reproduced from the given formula.
evidence: The estimated PPVs (positive predictive values) are derived assuming α = 0.05 for a single study.
PPV = ([1 − β]R + uβR)/(R + α − βR + u − uα + uβR)

llm_ocr|claim_audit_v3_quote_or_skip|cla.overall_comment: The algebra is sound and Table 4 reproduces exactly. Two slips: a missing parenthesis in Table 2, and a Box 1 ten-team PPV (1.5e-4) that the paper's own formula puts at about 2.5e-4. The headline 'most findings are false' is a consequence of assumed, unestimated pre-study odds and bias levels and of counting scenarios rather than findings, so it is a plausible argument, not a demonstrated quantity.

headline.answer: Using PPV = (1 − β)R/(R − βR + α) extended for bias u, Table 4 (p. 5) computes that only 2 of 9 typical design/setting scenarios reach PPV above 0.5 (adequately powered RCT and confirmatory meta-analysis, both 0.85), with others ranging from 0.41 down to 0.0010, supporting the claim that 'for most study designs and settings, it is more likely for a research claim to be false than true' (Abstract; section 'Most Research Findings Are False...').
headline.rationale: The title and abstract claim is qualitative ('most'), but its only quantitative support is the Table 4 PPV grid; the 0.85 RCT figure and the sub-0.5 values for the remaining scenarios are the headline numbers.
evidence: Simulations show that for most study designs and settings, it is more likely for a research claim to be false than true.
A finding from a well-conducted, adequately powered randomized controlled trial starting with a 50% pre-study chance that the intervention is effective is eventually true about 85% of the time.
In the described framework, a PPV exceeding 50% is quite difficult to get.

items.title: Headline 'most findings are false' rests on assumed, not estimated, R, power and u
items.location: Table 4; section 'Most Research Findings Are False for Most Research Designs and for Most Fields'
items.description: Every PPV in Table 4 is a deterministic function of the input values chosen for each 'Practical Example'. No empirical source is given for the assigned R (e.g. 1:5 for phase I/II RCTs, 1:10 for epidemiology) or u (0.2-0.8). The conclusion that most findings are false is therefore a restatement of the chosen inputs; the author himself concedes these are subjective.
items.quote: Even though these assumptions would be considerably subjective, they would still be very useful in interpreting research claims and putting them in context.

items.title: 'Most' across designs is not weighted by how many findings each design produces
items.description: Table 4 lists 9 scenarios, 7 with PPV < 0.5, but the claim that most published findings are false requires weighting scenarios by their share of published claims. Counting scenarios (not findings) does not establish the population-level 'most'; the share of the literature in each scenario is never estimated.
items.quote: Simulations show that for most study designs and settings, it is more likely for a research claim to be false than true.

items.title: Claim of proof outruns a conditional model
items.description: The model only shows PPV < 0.5 when (1 − β)R < α (or bias/multiple testing are large). Whether real fields satisfy those conditions is an empirical question not proven anywhere in the paper.
items.quote: It can be proven that most claimed research findings are false.

items.title: Box 1 ten-team PPV does not follow from the paper's own Table 3 formula
items.description: With R = 10^-4, power 0.60, α = 0.05, n = 10, the Table 3 formula PPV = R(1 − β^n)/(R + 1 − [1 − α]^n − Rβ^n) gives 1e-4 × 0.9999 / 0.4014 ≈ 2.5 × 10^-4, not 1.5 × 10^-4. Reproducing 1.5e-4 would need roughly n ≈ 30. The other Box 1 numbers (12 × 10^-4 without bias, 4.4 × 10^-4 with u = 0.10) do reproduce.
items.quote: if one of them finds a formally statistically significant association, the probability that the research finding is true is only 1.5 × 10⁻⁴

items.title: Table 2 cell is missing parentheses
items.description: The cell reads cα + uc(1 − α)/(R + 1); for the row to sum to the stated total c(R + α − βR + u − uα + uβR)/(R + 1), it must be (cα + uc(1 − α))/(R + 1). Typesetting error confirmed in the table image; the text PPV formula is correct.

items.title: Bias model assumes u is independent of truth and applies to all non-significant analyses
items.description: u converts a fixed fraction of all would-be-negative analyses into findings regardless of whether a true relationship exists. Table 4 then uses u as high as 0.8 (80% of non-findings reported as findings). Both the functional form and the magnitudes are asserted, and they drive the low-PPV rows (e.g. 0.17 vs 0.23 for the same RCT with u 0.8 vs 0.2).
items.quote: We may assume that u does not depend on whether a true relationship exists or not.

items.title: Multiple-team model treats 'at least one significant study' as the claimed finding
items.location: Section 'Testing by Several Independent Teams'; Table 3; Figure 2
items.description: The n-study PPV assumes the field credits a relationship whenever any one of n studies is significant, ignoring the other n − 1 results. Where the null studies are visible or meta-analysed, this overstates the false-positive share; the paper itself later argues the totality of evidence is what matters.
items.quote: The probability that at least one study, among several done on the same question, claims a statistically significant research finding is easy to estimate.

items.title: 'Barely crossing 0.05' computed with the p < α tail formula
items.description: The 12-fold update is the p ≤ 0.05 (tail-area) PPV, which is not the evidential value of a p-value just at 0.05. A finding with p barely at 0.05 carries less evidence than the tail calculation implies, so the stated number is mislabelled (if anything it is optimistic, which understates the author's point).
items.quote: if a statistically significant association is found with the p-value barely crossing the 0.05 threshold, the post-study probability that this is true increases about 12-fold

items.title: Analytical evaluations described as 'simulations'
items.description: Table 4 values are closed-form evaluations of the PPV formula (all nine reproduce to two decimals), not simulations; the wording suggests an empirical or stochastic exercise that was not done.
items.quote: Table 4 provides the results of simulations using the formulas developed for the influence of power, ratio of true to non-true relationships, and bias

problems.rationale: I recomputed all nine Table 4 PPVs from the Table 2 formula (0.8497, 0.8521, 0.4055, 0.2308, 0.1718, 0.2043, 0.1161, 0.0010, 0.0015), and they match. I also checked the bias-monotonicity condition (PPV falls in u iff 1 − β > α), which is correct, and the Box 1 numbers: 1.2e-3 and 4.4e-4 reproduce, but 1.5e-4 for ten teams does not (formula gives about 2.5e-4). The arithmetic is otherwise sound. The substantive problems are that the headline depends on unestimated input parameters and on scenario counting.
evidence: Even though these assumptions would be considerably subjective
It can be proven that most claimed research findings are false.
the probability that the research finding is true is only 1.5 × 10⁻⁴

headline_survives.rationale: The math is correct and the Table 4 numbers reproduce exactly, so the conditional claim (low R, low power, bias imply low PPV) stands. The leap to 'most published findings are false' depends on assumed R and u values and on unweighted scenario counting, neither of which the paper supports empirically. The direction is plausible for low-prior fields, but the magnitude and the 'most' are not established.
evidence: Simulations show that for most study designs and settings, it is more likely for a research claim to be false than true.
Even though these assumptions would be considerably subjective

replicability.rationale: The formulas, α = 0.05 and every input in Table 4 are given, and I reproduced all nine PPVs. Figures 1 and 2 are fully specified by their formulas. Two things are lost: the Box 1 ten-team value does not reproduce, and the choice of input parameters for each 'practical example' cannot be traced to any data.
evidence: The estimated PPVs (positive predictive values) are derived assuming α = 0.05 for a single study.
PPV = ([1 − β]R + uβR)/(R + α − βR + u − uα + uβR)

items.title: Box 1 ten-team PPV does not match the paper's own formula
items.location: Box 1, last paragraph; Table 3 / n-study PPV formula
items.description: With R=1e-4, power 0.60 (beta=0.4), alpha=0.05, n=10: PPV = R(1-0.4^10)/(R+1-0.95^10-R*0.4^10) = ~1.0e-4/(~0.4014) = ~2.5e-4, not 1.5e-4. The qualitative point (barely above the 1e-4 prior) survives, but the stated number is wrong.
items.quote: when ten independent research teams perform similar experiments around the world, if one of them finds a formally statistically significant association, the probability that the research finding is true is only 1.5 × 10⁻⁴

items.title: Overclaim of proof; conclusion depends on chosen R and u
items.description: 'Proven' is asserted, but the PPV is an algebraic identity whose value depends entirely on assumed R, power and u. Those inputs are hypothetical, not estimated from data, so the claim that most findings are false is an assumption-driven illustration rather than a demonstration.
items.quote: It can be proven that most claimed research findings are false.

items.title: 'Simulations' are deterministic formula evaluations with arbitrary inputs
items.location: Abstract; 'Most Research Findings Are False...' section; Table 4
items.description: Table 4 is described as simulation results, but it is closed-form evaluation of the PPV formula for hand-picked combinations of power, R and u (e.g. u=0.30 vs 0.40 vs 0.80) with no empirical grounding or sensitivity range. The mapping of study types to parameter values is asserted.
items.quote: Table 4 provides the results of simulations using the formulas developed for the influence of power, ratio of true to non-true relationships, and bias

items.title: Bias u assumed independent of truth and applied identically to all analyses
items.description: The model assumes bias converts the same proportion u of non-findings into findings whether or not the relationship is true, justified only by 'impossible to know'. This is a convenient assumption that drives the PPV reductions in Table 4 and Figure 1 and is not examined.
items.quote: We may assume that u does not depend on whether a true relationship exists or not.

items.title: Multiple-team model counts any one significant result as the finding
items.location: Testing by Several Independent Teams; Table 3
items.description: PPV for n studies conditions on at least one study being significant and ignores that the other n-1 studies would report nonsignificant results and so refute it; it also assumes independent, equal-power, unbiased studies. The result that PPV falls with n therefore depends on the 'unilateral attention' assumption, and Corollary 6 inherits this.
items.quote: The probability that at least one study, among several done on the same question, claims a statistically significant research finding is easy to estimate.

items.title: Empirical figures given without support
items.description: Quantitative anchors such as 100-fold smaller samples and relative risks 3-20 for smoking vs cancer/cardiovascular disease are stated with only a general citation or none; smoking-CVD relative risks are generally much lower than 3. These are used to rank fields but not verified.
items.quote: such as the impact of smoking on cancer or cardiovascular disease (relative risks 3–20)

items.title: Figure panel order differs from caption
items.description: Caption says panels correspond to power 0.20, 0.50 and 0.80, but panels A, B, C in the image are power 80%, 50%, 20%.
items.quote: Panels correspond to power of 0.20, 0.50, and 0.80.

items.title: Model is about all tested relationships, not published ones
items.description: R is defined over relationships tested in a field and PPV over those reaching significance; the title claims this applies to 'published' findings, with no model of publication selection beyond u. Table 4 PPVs are not tied to any observed share of published findings.
items.quote: Let R be the ratio of the number of “true relationships” to “no relationships” among those tested in the field.

problems.rationale: I re-computed all nine Table 4 PPVs, the Box 1 12-fold and 4.4e-4 values, and the Figure 1/2 endpoints; they match. The one arithmetic error is the 1.5e-4 in Box 1. The substantive problems are assumption-dependence and overclaiming.
evidence: It can be proven that most claimed research findings are false.
the probability that the research finding is true is only 1.5 × 10⁻⁴

headline_survives.rationale: The arithmetic behind Table 4 is correct, so the PPV values follow from the stated inputs. What remains uncertain is whether the inputs (R, u, power) represent real fields, so the direction is plausible but the magnitude and 'proven' language are not established.
evidence: PPV for each claimed relationship is extremely low
Even though these assumptions would be considerably subjective

replicability.rationale: All formulas, 2x2 tables, and parameter values for Table 4 and Box 1 are given; I reproduced every Table 4 entry by hand. Deductions: no code, and the mapping from study type to R and u is not justified; Box 1's 1.5e-4 does not reproduce.
evidence: The estimated PPVs (positive predictive values) are derived assuming α = 0.05 for a single study.

items.title: Empirical conclusion rests on assumed, not estimated, parameters
items.location: Table 4; 'Most Research Findings Are False' section
items.description: The PPV framework is appropriate for showing how power, pre-study odds, bias and multiplicity combine, but the key inputs (R, u for each 'practical example') are asserted without empirical calibration, so the design cannot by itself establish what fraction of the actual literature is false.
items.quote: Table 4 provides the results of simulations using the formulas developed for the influence of power, ratio of true to non-true relationships, and bias

items.title: Binary true/false and threshold-based significance model
items.description: Findings are dichotomized at p<0.05 and relationships as exactly true or null; effect-size accuracy and degree of truth are outside the model, limiting what 'false' means.
items.quote: Research findings are defined here as any relationship reaching formal statistical significance

items.title: Bias assumed independent of truth status
items.description: u is assumed equal for true and null relationships; justified only by the remark that truth is unknown, which does not imply bias acts equally.
items.quote: We may assume that u does not depend on whether a true relationship exists or not.

design.rationale: As an analytic/modeling essay, the 2x2 Bayesian PPV design (Tables 1-3) is well suited to deriving the qualitative corollaries; Figures 1-2 show the expected monotone effects of u and n across power levels. But the paper's headline is an empirical claim about the published literature, and no data are collected to estimate R, u, or power distributions in real fields. The design answers 'under what conditions' well, and 'how often in reality' weakly.
evidence: Let us also consider, for computational simplicity, circumscribed fields where either there is only one true relationship (among many that can be hypothesized) or the power is similar
Thus, it is unavoidable that one should make approximate assumptions on how many relationships are expected to be true among those probed

items.title: Box 1 multi-team PPV does not match the paper's own formula
items.description: With R = 1e-4, power 0.6, alpha 0.05, n = 10, the Table 3 formula R(1-β^n)/(R+1-(1-α)^n-Rβ^n) gives about 2.5e-4, not the 1.5e-4 stated. Qualitative point unchanged.
items.quote: the probability that the research finding is true is only 1.5 × 10⁻⁴

items.title: Table 2 cell missing parentheses
items.description: The false-positive cell is printed as cα + uc(1 − α)/(R + 1); it should be (cα + uc(1 − α))/(R + 1) for the row total and the PPV formula in the text to follow.

items.title: 'Simulations' are deterministic plug-in calculations without uncertainty
items.description: Table 4 values are single point evaluations of a closed-form formula at chosen inputs; no sensitivity ranges or uncertainty over the inputs are reported, though calling them simulations suggests more.
items.quote: Simulations show that for most study designs and settings, it is more likely for a research claim to be false than true.

items.title: Box 1 mixes 'p barely crossing 0.05' with threshold-based PPV
items.description: The 12-fold update is computed from the α-threshold PPV (0.6R/(0.6R+0.05) ≈ 12e-4), which is the probability given p<0.05, not given p just at 0.05; the wording conflates the two.

items.title: Unsupported generalization to 'the majority of modern biomedical research'
items.description: No data establish that most research operates at low R or high u; this is asserted as already 'shown'.
items.quote: As shown, the majority of modern biomedical research is operating in areas with very low pre- and post-study probability for true findings.

items.title: Effect sizes as 'accurate measures' of bias
items.description: Holds only in a hypothetical null field; generalizing that large effects are more likely bias 'in most fields' is speculative.
items.quote: Too large and too highly significant effects may actually be more likely to be signs of large bias in most fields of modern research.

claims.rationale: Much of the body is appropriately hedged ('may', 'probably'), and the corollaries follow from the formulas. But the title, the introduction's 'It can be proven', and the abstract's 'Simulations show that for most study designs and settings' present a conditional model output as an established empirical fact. Table 4 itself shows two of nine scenarios with PPV 0.85, and the 'most designs' conclusion depends on which scenarios were chosen and their assumed u values.
evidence: In this framework, a research finding is less likely to be true when the studies conducted in a field are smaller
In the described framework, a PPV exceeding 50% is quite difficult to get.
I suspect several established "classics" will fail the test [36].

transparency.rationale: Pre-registration and code/data availability are largely not applicable to an analytic essay. All formulas, 2x2 tables, and the exact parameter combinations in Table 4 are reported, so every number can be reproduced by hand (I did so). Weaknesses: the parameter values per scenario are not justified or sourced, no sensitivity analysis is given, and Figure curves are not accompanied by code; minor typesetting/arithmetic errors reduce reproducibility slightly.
evidence: Assuming that c relationships are being probed in the field, the expected values of the 2 × 2 table are given in Table 1.
The estimated PPVs (positive predictive values) are derived assuming α = 0.05 for a single study.

novelty.rationale: The base PPV framework is explicitly credited to prior work (Wacholder et al., Risch, Sterne & Davey Smith). The new contributions are the explicit bias parameter u, the multiple-independent-teams extension, the six corollaries, and the 'null field' idea that claimed effects measure net bias. These are a meaningful and well-synthesized extension, though mathematically modest.
evidence: As has been shown previously, the probability that a research finding is indeed true depends on the prior probability of it being true (before doing the study), the statistical power of the study, and the level of statistical significance [10,11].
What is less well appreciated is that bias and the extent of repeated independent testing by different teams of investigators around the globe may further distort this picture
This concept totally reverses the way we view scientific results.

items.title: No acknowledgment that the parameter values are guesses
items.description: The paper never states that the R and u values assigned to each design are unvalidated, nor how conclusions change under other plausible values.
items.quote: for various types of situations that may be characteristic of specific study designs and settings

limitations.rationale: Some real caveats are named: corollaries interact and can offset each other, reverse bias exists, the gold standard is unattainable, and assumptions about pre-study odds are 'considerably subjective'. However, the central limitation, that the empirical conclusion depends on unmeasured parameter values chosen by the author, is not confronted, and model simplifications (dichotomous truth, u independent of truth, equal power) are introduced as conveniences rather than discussed as limitations.
evidence: These corollaries consider each factor separately, but these factors often influence each other.
Even though these assumptions would be considerably subjective, they would still be very useful in interpreting research claims
There is no good large-scale empirical evidence on how frequently such reverse bias may occur across diverse research fields.

items.description: The claim that most published findings are false is a property of the model only for the chosen inputs (R, power, u). items.title: Box 1 assumes alpha=0.05 for a 100,000-SNP genome-wide scan
items.description: The 12 x 10^-4 PPV assumes each of 100,000 polymorphisms is tested at alpha=0.05 with no multiplicity correction. That means about 5,000 expected false positives, which makes the example very pessimistic. Genome-wide studies normally use much stricter thresholds. The paper itself cites a multiple-testing literature [37], but the worked example does not use it.
items.quote: Let us also suppose that the study has 60% power to find an association with an odds ratio of 1.3 at α = 0.05.

items.title: 'Barely crossing 0.05' is conflated with 'p < 0.05'
items.description: The PPV formula conditions on the event p <= alpha, which averages over all significant results. A result with p just at 0.05 has a lower likelihood ratio than that average, so the 12-fold increase applies to 'any significant result', not to one 'barely crossing' the threshold.
items.quote: if a statistically significant association is found with the p-value barely crossing the 0.05 threshold, the post-study probability that this is true increases about 12-fold

items.title: Bias model assumes u is independent of truth, and the multi-team model treats 'any one significant' as the finding
items.location: Bias section; Testing by Several Independent Teams
items.description: u is applied equally to true and null relationships ('We may assume that u does not depend on whether a true relationship exists'). The n-team model counts a claim as true or false when at least one of n studies is significant, ignoring the other n-1 (non-significant) reports. Both are simplifying assumptions that push PPV downward, and the paper does not test how sensitive its conclusions are to them.
items.quote: We may assume that u does not depend on whether a true relationship exists or not.

items.title: Reverse bias dismissed without evidence

items.title: Box 1 multi-team PPV (1.5 x 10^-4) does not follow from the paper's own Table 3 formula
items.description: With R = 1e-4, power 0.6 (beta = 0.4), alpha = 0.05, n = 10, the stated formula PPV = R(1 - beta^n)/(R + 1 - [1 - alpha]^n - R beta^n) gives about 2.5 x 10^-4, not 1.5 x 10^-4. items.title: Box 1 applies the p <= 0.05 PPV to a p-value 'barely crossing' 0.05
items.description: The 12-fold update (PPV of about 1.2e-3, which checks arithmetically) comes from the Table 1 formula, which conditions on p < alpha, i.e. any significant result. A p-value just at 0.05 carries a smaller likelihood ratio than the average significant result. So the text misdescribes the calculation, and the true update for a borderline p would be smaller still.

items.description: Table 3 classifies a question as a 'research finding' if any of n studies is significant, regardless of how many were negative. Figure 2 and Corollary 6 therefore model a worst-case reading practice, not the PPV of the literature.

items.description: As printed, the cell reads c*alpha + uc(1 - alpha)/(R + 1). For the row total to add up, it must be (c*alpha + uc(1 - alpha))/(R + 1). This is a typesetting slip; the PPV formula in the text is correct.

items.title: Significance treated as a yes/no threshold, ignoring the actual p-value
items.description: The PPV counts any finding with p < 0.05 as positive, so a finding with p = 0.001 is treated the same as one at p = 0.049. This understates PPV for findings with strong evidence and may push the headline toward 'false'.
items.quote: Research findings are defined here as any relationship reaching formal statistical significance

items.title: Unsupported claim that reverse bias is uncommon
items.description: The model leaves out reverse bias by assertion, even though the paper admits there is no data on it. Leaving it out pushes the estimated PPV down.
items.quote: There is no good large-scale empirical evidence on how frequently such reverse bias may occur across diverse research fields. However, it is probably fair to say that reverse bias is not as common.

headline.answer: Most claimed research findings are false: under the PPV model with bias, PPV exceeds 0.5 only in 2 of 9 illustrative scenarios in Table 4 (p.5), e.g. 0.85 for an adequately powered RCT with 1:1 odds vs 0.20 for an adequately powered exploratory epidemiological study and 0.0010-0.0015 for discovery-oriented research.
headline.rationale: The title claim is operationalized through the PPV formulas and the Table 4 scenarios.
evidence: It can be proven that most claimed research findings are false.
In the described framework, a PPV exceeding 50% is quite difficult to get.

items.title: 'Proven' overclaims a conditional result
items.location: Introduction; Most Research Findings Are False section
items.description: The formulas only show PPV < 0.5 for chosen R, power and u values; whether 'most' findings are false depends on the empirical distribution of those parameters across published research, which the paper never estimates. The mathematical result is conditional, not a proof of the empirical claim.
items.quote: It can be proven that most claimed research findings are false.

items.title: Table 4 parameters (R, u) are asserted, not sourced
items.description: Values like u = 0.30 for a confirmatory meta-analysis, u = 0.80 for poorly performed trials, or R = 1:10 for epidemiology have no cited empirical basis, yet they drive every PPV in the table. The headline rests on these assumptions.
items.quote: Table 4 provides the results of simulations using the formulas developed for the influence of power, ratio of true to non-true relationships, and bias

items.title: 'Most' not weighted by volume of research
items.location: Most Research Findings Are False section; Table 4
items.description: Table 4 lists 9 unweighted scenarios; concluding that most findings are false requires knowing what share of published findings come from each design, which is not provided.
items.quote: Simulations show that for most study designs and settings, it is more likely for a research claim to be false than true.

items.title: 'Simulations' are deterministic formula evaluations
items.description: Table 4 values are closed-form PPV calculations (I re-derived all 9 and they match), not simulations; the label suggests more empirical grounding than exists.
items.quote: Simulations show that for most study designs and settings

items.title: Dichotomizing at p < 0.05 discards evidential strength
items.description: A 'finding' is any p < 0.05 result, so a p = 0.001 result is treated identically to p = 0.049; this inflates the false share relative to a model using observed p-values, and the multiple-team model treats only 'at least one significant' as the claim, ignoring the visible negative studies.
items.quote: Research findings are defined here as any relationship reaching formal statistical significance

items.title: Notation slips (a vs alpha; < vs <=)
items.location: Modeling and Testing by Several Independent Teams sections
items.description: Alpha is written as 'a' and the condition is stated as '1 - β ≤ α' in one place and '1 - β < a' in another.
items.quote: unless 1 - β < a, i.e., typically 1 − β < 0.05

problems.rationale: Arithmetic in Table 4 and Tables 1-3 checks out; the problems are in the leap from conditional formulas with assumed parameters to an empirical 'most'.
evidence: It can be proven that most claimed research findings are false.

headline_survives.rationale: The math and Table 4 numbers are correct, but the 'most findings are false' magnitude rests on unsourced R and u values and an unweighted set of scenarios, so direction is plausible for low-prior fields while the overall magnitude is uncertain.
evidence: In the described framework, a PPV exceeding 50% is quite difficult to get.

replicability.rationale: Every Table 4 PPV can be reproduced exactly from the given formula and listed parameters; what cannot be reproduced is how the parameter values or the field-level 'most' claim were derived.

headline.answer: Under the paper's PPV framework, a claimed finding is true with probability PPV = ([1-β]R + uβR)/(R+α-βR+u-uα+uβR). For most plausible combinations of power, pre-study odds R and bias u, PPV is below 50%. Table 4 gives, for example, 0.20 for a well-powered exploratory epidemiological study (R=1:10, u=0.30) and 0.0010 to 0.0015 for discovery-oriented research (R=1:1000). The best cases, an adequately powered RCT and a confirmatory meta-analysis, reach 0.85.
